question: Onwhat headings will the magnetic compass read most accurately during a level 360° turn, with a bank of approximately 15°?

answers.C: 135° through 225°.

explanations.A:
because compass turning errors are
greatest at north and south headings.
explanations.B:
In a turn through north or south, the
compass indication will usually be incorrect. But in a turn through
east or west, the compass indication is usually accurate.
Therefore, the compass should be indicating properly when

passing through 90° and 270°. This holds true for only medium to
‘shallow bank turns, e.g., 15-30°.
explanations.C:
because the compass leads the heading
in a turn through south.

question: What causes the northerly turning error in a magnetic compass?

answers.A: Coriolis force at the mid-latitudes.
answers.B: The magnetic dip characteristic.
answers.C: Centrifugal force acting on the compass card.

explanations.A:
because the Coriolis force of the spinning
Earth affects winds rather than compass indications.
explanations.B:
Magnetic dip causes a compass needle to

point both down toward the earth and to the magnetic pole. This
characteristic causes turning errors.
explanations.C:
because centrifugal force is not related to
compass turning errors.

question: During flight, if the pitot tube becomes clogged with ice, which of the following instruments would be affected?

answers.A: The airspeed indicator and the altimeter.
answers.B: The airspeed indicator only.
answers.C: The airspeed indicator, altimeter, and Vertical Speed Indicator.

explanations.A:
because the pitot tube is connected only
to the airspeed indicator, not the altimeter.
explanations.B:
The pitot-static system is a source of
pressure for the altimeter, vertical speed indicator, and airspeed
indicator. The pitot tube is connected directly to the airspeed
indicator, and the static vents are connected directly to all three.
The pressure of air coming into the pitot tube (impact air
pressure) is compared with the air pressure at the static system
vents to determine airspeed.
explanations.C:
because the pitot tube is connected only

to the airspeed indicator, not the altimeter or vertical speed
indicator.

question: If both the ram air input and the drain hole of the pitot system are blocked, what reaction should you observe on the airspeed indicator when power is applied and a climb is initiated out of severe icing conditions?

answers.A: No change until an actual climb rate is established, then indicated airspeed will increase.
answers.B: The indicated airspeed would show a continuous deceleration while climbing.
answers.C: The airspeed would drop to, and remain at, zero.

explanations.A:
When the airspeed indicator pitot tube and
drain hole are blocked, the airspeed indicator will react as an
altimeter. There will be a constant pressure within the pitot tube,
and as the pressure from the static source decreases during a
climb, the indicated airspeed on the altimeter will increase.
explanations.B:
because, as there is an increase in
altitude, the airspeed indicator will show an increase in airspeed
as the air pressure within the pitot tube is relatively greater than
that of the static air.
explanations.C:
because this reaction would occur if the
ram air input, but not the drain hole, were blocked.

question: What indication should a pilot observe if an airspeed indicator ram air input and drain hole are blocked?

answers.A: The airspeed indicator will react as an altimeter.
answers.B: No airspeed indicator change will occur during climbs or descents.
answers.C: The airspeed indicator will show a decrease with an increase in altitude.

explanations.A:
When the airspeed indicator pitot tube and
drain hole are blocked, the airspeed indicator will react as an
altimeter. There will be a constant pressure within the pitot tube,
and as the pressure from the static source decreases during a
climb, the indicated airspeed on the altimeter will increase.
explanations.B:
because differential pressure between

the pitot tube and static air source changes, and so does
indicated airspeed.
explanations.C:
because indicated airspeed will
increase, not decrease, with increases in altitude.

question: If both the ram air input and drain hole of the pitot system are blocked, what airspeed indication can be expected?

answers.A: No variation of indicated airspeed in level flight even if large power changes are made.
answers.B: Decrease of indicated airspeed during a climb.
answers.C: Constant indicated airspeed during a descent.

explanations.A:
If both the pitot tube input and the drain

hole on the pitot system are blocked, the airspeed indication will
be constant at any given altitude.
explanations.B:
because, during a climb, the airspeed
indicator will indicate an increase, not decrease, due to the

stronger differential pressure in the blocked pitot tube relative to
the static vents.
explanations.C:
because indicated airspeed would
change with changes in altitude.

question: Ifthe outside air temperature increases during a flight at constant power and at a constant indicated altitude, the true airspeed will

answers.B: increase and true altitude will increase.
answers.C: decrease and true altitude will increase.
answers.A: increase and true altitude will decrease.

explanations.A:
because true altitude increases, not

decreases.
explanations.B:
As temperature increases, pressure levels
rise farther above sea level and true altitude increases given a

constant indicated altitude. As altitude increases with constant
power, true airspeed increases.
explanations.C: because TAS increases, not decreases.

question: If, while in level flight, it becomes necessary to use an alternate source of static pressure vented inside the airplane, which of the following should the pilot expect?

answers.A: The vertical speed to momentarily show a descent.
answers.B: The altimeter to read higher than normal.
answers.C: The vertical speed to show a climb.

explanations.A:
because the VSI indication will be a
momentary climb, not a descent.
explanations.B:
Most aircraft equipped with a pitot-static
system are provided with an alternate source of static pressure
for emergency use. This source is usually vented inside the
cabin. The pressure within an unpressurized cockpit is slightly
lower than the pressure outside the airplane because of the
Venturi effect of the air moving past the outside of the cockpit.
When the alternate static source is used, the altimeter and
airspeed indicator will read higher than actual, and the vertical
speed indicator will momentarily show a climb.
explanations.C:
because the VSI will show only a
momentary, not a steady-state, climb.

question: If while in level flight, it becomes necessary to use an alternate source of static pressure vented inside the airplane, which of the following variations in instrument indications should the pilot expect?

answers.A: The altimeter will read higher than normal, airspeed greater than normal, and the VSI will momentarily show a climb.
answers.B: The altimeter will read lower than normal, airspeed greater than normal, and the VSI will momentarily show a climb and then a descent.
answers.C: The altimeter will read lower than normal, airspeed lower than normal, and the VSI will momentarily show a descent.

explanations.A:
Most aircraft equipped with a pitot-static
system are provided with an alternate source of static pressure
for emergency use. This source is usually vented inside the
cabin. The pressure within an unpressurized cockpit is slightly
lower than the pressure outside the airplane because of the
Venturi effect of the air moving past the outside of the cockpit.
When the alternate static source is used, the altimeter will read
higher than actual, and the vertical speed indicator will
momentarily show a climb.
explanations.B:
because the altimeter will read higher, not
lower, than normal, and the vertical speed indicator will show
level flight, not a descent, after the momentary climb.
explanations.C:
because the altimeter and airspeed
indicators will read higher, not lower, than normal, and the vertical
speed indicator will momentarily show a climb, not a descent.

question: If, while in level flight, it becomes necessary to use an alternate source of static pressure vented inside the airplane, which of the following should the pilot expect?

answers.B: The gyroscopic instruments to become inoperative.
answers.C: The altimeter and airspeed indicator to become inoperative.
answers.A: The vertical speed to momentarily show a climb.

explanations.A:
Most aircraft equipped with a pitot-static
system are provided with an alternate source of static pressure
for emergency use. This source is usually vented inside the
cabin. The pressure within an unpressurized cockpit is slightly
lower than the pressure outside the airplane because of the
Venturi effect of the air moving past the outside of the cockpit.
When the alternate static source is used, the altimeter and
airspeed indicator will read higher than actual, and the vertical
speed indicator will momentarily show a climb.
explanations.B:
because the gyroscopic instruments are
not affected by changes in the pitot-static system.
explanations.C:
because the altimeter and airspeed
indicator will read higher than actual, not become inoperative.

question: What would be the indication on the VSI during entry into a 500 FPM actual descent from level flight if the static ports were iced over?

answers.B: The indication would be in reverse of the actual rate of descent (500 FPM climb).
answers.C: The VSI pointer would remain at zero regardless of the actual rate of descent.
answers.A: The initial indication would be a climb, then descent at a rate in excess of 500 FPM.

explanations.A:
because, with no change in pressure, the
indication would be level flight, not a climb or descent.
explanations.B:
because, with no change in pressure, the
indication would be level flight, not a climb.
explanations.C:
The vertical speed indicator operates from
the static pressure source and indicates change in pressure.
Thus, if the static pressure ports became iced over, there would

be no change in the static pressure, and there would be no
indication of descent or climb.

question: You check the flight instruments while taxiing and find the vertical speed indicator (VSI) indicates a descent of 100 feet per minute. In this case, you

answers.A: may take off and use 100 feet descent as the zero indication.
answers.B: must return to the parking area and have the instrument corrected by an authorized instrument repairman.
answers.C: may not take off until the instrument is corrected by either the pilot or a mechanic.

explanations.A:
The needle of the vertical speed indicator
(VSI) should indicate zero when the aircraft is on the ground or is
maintaining a constant pressure level in flight. If it does not
indicate zero, you must allow for the error when interpreting the
indications in flight. Since the VSI is not a required instrument,
you may fly when it is out of adjustment.
explanations.B:
because the VSI can be used by making
allowances in flight.
explanations.C:
because the VSI can be used by making
allowances in flight.

question: What information does a Mach meter present?

answers.A: The ratio of aircraft equivalent airspeed, corrected for installation error, to the speed of sound.
answers.B: The ratio of aircraft indicated airspeed to the speed of sound.
answers.C: The ratio of aircraft true airspeed to the speed of sound.

explanations.A:
because equivalent airspeed is the
calibrated airspeed of an aircraft corrected for compressibility
flow at a particular altitude. The Mach meter uses true airspeed.
explanations.B:
because the Mach meter uses true
airspeed, not indicated airspeed.
explanations.C:
The Mach meter indicates the ratio of
aircraft true airspeed to the speed of sound at flight altitude. It
uses the pressure differential between the impact and static air
sources and corrects automatically for temperature and altitude.

question: How should you preflight check the altimeter prior to an IFR flight?

answers.A: Set the altimeter first with 29.92" Hg and then the current altimeter setting. The change in altitude should correspond to the change in setting.
answers.B: Set the altimeter to the current altimeter setting. The indication should be within 75 feet of the actual elevation for acceptable accuracy.
answers.C: Set the altimeter to 29.92" Hg. With current temperature and the altimeter indication, determine the true altitude to compare with the field elevation.

explanations.A:
because only indicated altitude, not
change in altitude, is checked.
explanations.B:
Set the altimeter to the local altimeter
setting before taking off, and verify that the indication is within 75
ft. of the actual elevation. If the difference is greater than 75 ft.,
you should consult an instrument repair shop.
explanations.C:
because setting the altimeter to 29.92

and adjusting for temperature gives density altitude, not true
altitude.

question: How should you preflight check the altimeter prior to an IFR flight?

answers.A: Set the altimeter to the current altimeter setting. The indication should be within 75 feet of the actual elevation for acceptable accuracy.
answers.B: Set the altimeter first with 29.92" Hg and then the current altimeter setting. The change in altitude should correspond to the change in setting.
answers.C: Set the altimeter to the current temperature. With current temperature and the altimeter indication, determine the calibrated altitude to compare with the field elevation.

explanations.A:
Set the altimeter to the local altimeter
setting before taking off, and verify that the indication is within 75
ft. of the actual elevation. If the difference is greater than 75 ft.,
you should consult an instrument repair shop.
explanations.B:
because only indicated altitude, not
change in altitude, is checked.
explanations.C:
because an altimeter can be adjusted for
nonstandard pressure, not temperature.

question: Pressure altitude is the altitude read on your altimeter when the instrument is adjusted to indicate height above

answers.A: the standard datum plane.
answers.B: sea level.
answers.C: ground level.

explanations.A:
Pressure altitude is the altitude read on
your altimeter when the instrument is adjusted to indicate height
above the standard datum plane, i.e., an altimeter setting of
29.92 in. The standard datum plane is a theoretical level where
the weight of the atmosphere is 29.92 in. of Hg.
explanations.B:
because indicated altitude, not pressure
altitude, is the altitude read on your altimeter (when set to the
correct altimeter setting) to indicate the approximate height
above mean sea level.
explanations.C:
because the height above ground
(absolute altitude) may be indicated directly on a radar altimeter,
not by adjusting a pressure altimeter to 29.92 in.

question: The local altimeter setting should be used by all pilots in a particular area, primarily to provide for

answers.B: the cancellation of altimeter error due to nonstandard temperatures aloft.
answers.C: better vertical separation of aircraft.
answers.A: more accurate terrain clearance in mountainous areas.

explanations.A:
because temperatures aloft must also be
considered to assure terrain clearance.
explanations.B:
because the altimeter setting does not
compensate for nonstandard temperatures aloft. Rather, all
altimeters in the area will reflect the same uncompensated
amount.
explanations.C:
Because the altimeter in each airplane is
equally affected by temperature and pressure variation errors,
use of the local altimeter setting in a given area provides for
better vertical separation of aircraft.

because, in altimeter 1, both the thin hand

because, in altimeter 3, the short hand is

question: Altimeter setting is the value to which the scale of the pressure altimeter is set so the altimeter indicates

answers.B: pressure altitude at sea level.
answers.C: pressure altitude at field elevation.
answers.A: true altitude at field elevation.

explanations.A:
The altimeter setting is the value which
permits the altimeter to indicate the true altitude at field elevation.
Within the vicinity of a particular airport, the altimeter setting
provides an accurate means of separating traffic vertically and
also provides obstruction clearance. Note that the use of the
word "true" here is not completely accurate because the altimeter
setting does not correct for nonstandard temperature.
explanations.B:
because the altimeter setting causes the

altimeter to indicate true altitude, not pressure altitude, at field
elevation, not sea level.
explanations.C:
because the altimeter setting causes the
altimeter to indicate true altitude, not pressure altitude.

question: Altimeter setting is the value to which the scale of the pressure altimeter is set so the altimeter indicates

answers.A: pressure altitude at field elevation.
answers.B: pressure altitude at sea level.
answers.C: true altitude at field elevation.

explanations.A:
because the altimeter setting causes the
altimeter to indicate true altitude, not pressure altitude.
explanations.B:
because the altimeter setting causes the

altimeter to indicate true altitude, not pressure altitude, at field
elevation, not sea level.
explanations.C:
The altimeter setting is the value which
permits the altimeter to indicate the true altitude at field elevation.
Within the vicinity of a particular airport, the altimeter setting
provides an accurate means of separating traffic vertically and
also provides obstruction clearance. Note that the use of the
word "true" here is not completely accurate because the altimeter
setting does not correct for nonstandard temperature.

question: If you are departing from an airport where you cannot obtain an altimeter setting, you should set your altimeter

answers.B: on the current airport barometric pressure, if known.
answers.C: to the airport elevation.

explanations.A:
because setting the altimeter to 29.92
would provide only pressure altitude.
explanations.B:
because the altimeter setting is the
current barometric pressure adjusted to sea level.
explanations.C:
If you cannot obtain an altimeter setting at

an airport, adjust your altimeter so it reads the current airport
elevation.

question: Which altitude is indicated when the altimeter is set to 29.92" Hg?

answers.B: Standard.
answers.C: Density.
answers.A: Pressure.

explanations.A:
Pressure altitude is indicated when the
altimeter is set to 29.92.
explanations.B:
because standard altitude is a nonsense
concept in this context.
explanations.C:
because density altitude is pressure
altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature.

question: The pressure altitude at a given location is indicated on the altimeter after the altimeter is set to

answers.A: the current altimeter setting.
answers.B: the field elevation.

explanations.A:
because the altitude indicated on the

altimeter after it is set to the current altimeter setting is the
indicated altitude, not pressure altitude.
explanations.B:
because you set the altimeter to a
barometric pressure, not an elevation.
explanations.C:
Pressure altitude by definition is indicated
altitude when the altimeter setting is 29.92. This is true
regardless of area or true altitude.

question: How can you determine the pressure altitude on an airport without a tower or FSS?

answers.A: Set the altimeter to 29.92" Hg and read the altitude indicated.
answers.B: Set the altimeter to the current altimeter setting of a station within 100 miles and correct this indicated altitude with local temperature.
answers.C: Use your computer and correct the field elevation for temperature.

explanations.A:
The pressure altitude is determined by
setting your altimeter to 29.92 and reading the altitude indicated.
No matter what altitude or location, the altimeter reads pressure
altitude when the barometric window is set to 29.92" Hg.
explanations.B: because it describes true altitude.
explanations.C:
because correcting field elevation for
temperature is a nonsense concept.

question: How can you obtain the pressure altitude on flights below 18,000 feet?

answers.A: Use your computer to change the indicated altitude to pressure altitude.
answers.B: Set your altimeter to 29.92" Hg.
answers.C: Contact an FSS and ask for the pressure altitude.

explanations.A:
because it is much easier to just change
the altimeter to 29.92.
explanations.B:
Pressure altitude can be determined
anywhere by setting the altimeter to 29.92.
explanations.C:
because pressure altitude is determined
by setting your altimeter to 29.92, not by contacting an FSS.

question: Atan altitude of 6,500 feet MSL, the current altimeter setting is 30.42" Hg. The pressure altitude would be approximately

answers.B: 7,500 feet.
answers.C: 6,000 feet.
answers.A: 6,500 feet.

explanations.A:
because pressure altitude is equal to
actual altitude only when the current altimeter setting is 29.92.
explanations.B:
because a pressure change of 0.5" Hg
results in an altitude change of 500 ft., not 1,000 ft.
explanations.C:
Rotating the altimeter's setting knob toa
higher (or lower) barometric setting moves the hands to higher
(or lower) indicated altitude at the rate of 1" Hg to 1,000 ft. of
altitude. Given the current altimeter setting of 30.42 and the
indicated altitude of 6,500 ft., resetting the window to 29.92
would lower indicated altitude by 500 ft. (30.42 - 29.92 = 0.5" Hg

= 500 ft.). The new indicated altitude would be 6,000 ft. MSL,
which would be pressure altitude.

question: How does a pilot normally obtain the current altimeter setting during anIFR flight in Class E airspace below 18,000 feet?

answers.A: ATC periodically advises the pilot of the proper altimeter setting.
answers.B: The pilot should contact ARTCC at least every 100 NM and request the altimeter setting.
answers.C: FSS's along the route broadcast the weather information at 15 minutes past the hour.

explanations.A:
During IFR flight in Class E airspace below
18,000 ft. MSL, ATC periodically provides altimeter settings.

Thus, you will continually hear the altimeter settings given to other
pilots as you monitor ATC.
explanations.B:
because ATC provides the altimeter
setting without being asked.
explanations.C:
because FSSs do not broadcast the
altimeter setting at 15 min. past the hour.

question: Which of the following defines the type of altitude used when maintaining FL 2102

answers.B: Calibrated.
answers.C: Pressure.
answers.A: Indicated.

explanations.A:
because indicated altitude is the altitude
shown on the altimeter after it is set to the current altimeter
setting. Pressure altitude, not indicated altitude, is used at or
above 18,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.B: because all altimeters are calibrated.
explanations.C:
Above 18,000 ft. MSL (FL 180), pressure
altitude is used to separate traffic. Pressure altitude is the
altitude indicated on an altimeter when it is set to 29.92.

question: What is the procedure for setting the altimeter when assigned an IFR altitude of 18,000 feet or higher on a direct flight off airways?

answers.A: Set the altimeter to the current reported setting for climb-out and 29.92" Hg upon reaching 18,000 feet.
answers.B: Set the altimeter to the current altimeter setting until reaching the assigned altitude, then set to 29.92" Hg.
answers.C: Set the altimeter to 29.92" Hg before takeoff.

explanations.A:
When you are at an altitude of 18,000 ft.
MSL (FL 180) or higher, the altimeter should be set to 29.92,
which is pressure altitude. It does not matter whether you are on
an airway.
explanations.B:
because you should set the altimeter to

29.92 upon reaching FL 180, not upon reaching your assigned
altitude.
explanations.C:
because indicated altitude (using local
altimeter settings) should be used up to FL 180.

question: While you are flying at FL 250, you hear ATC give an altimeter setting of 28.92" Hg in your area. At what pressure altitude are you flying?

explanations.A:
because FL 250 by definition means a
pressure altitude of 25,000 ft., not 24,000 ft.
explanations.B:
The pressure altitude is 25,000 ft. in your

area because at FL 250 your altimeter should be set at 29.92. A
flight level (FL) by definition means a pressure altitude.
explanations.C:
because FL 250 by definition means a
pressure altitude of 25,000 ft., not 26,000 ft.

question: Enroute at FL 290, the altimeter is set correctly, but not reset to the local altimeter setting of 30.57" Hg during descent. If the field elevation is 650 feet and the altimeter is functioning properly, what is the approximate indication upon landing?

answers.A: 715 feet.
answers.B: 1,300 feet.
answers.C: Sea level.

explanations.A:
because 715 ft. is obtained by adding 65
ft. rather than subtracting 650 ft.
explanations.B:
because 1,300 ft. is obtained by adding
650 ft. rather than subtracting 650 ft.
explanations.C:
One in. of pressure equals approximately
1,000 ft. of altitude. If an altimeter should be set to 30.57 but is
set to 29.92, it is set .65" Hg too low and thus will indicate 650 ft.
(1,000 ft. x .65) less than actual altitude. Thus, if the airplane
lands at an airport with a field elevation of 650 ft., the altimeter
will indicate sea level, i.e., 650 ft. elevation minus the 650 ft.
altimeter setting error.

question: Enroute at FL 290, your altimeter is set correctly, but you fail to reset it to the local altimeter setting of 30.26" Hg during descent. If the field elevation is 134 feet and your altimeter is functioning properly, what will it indicate after landing?

answers.A: 100 feet MSL.
answers.B: 474 feet MSL.
answers.C: 206 feet below MSL.

explanations.A:
because 100 ft. is obtained by
subtracting 34 ft. rather than subtracting 340 ft.
explanations.B:
because 474 ft. is obtained by adding
340 ft. rather than subtracting 340 ft.
explanations.C:
One in. of pressure equals approximately
1,000 ft. of altitude. If an altimeter should be set to 30.26 but is
set to 29.92, it is set 34" Hg too low and thus will indicate 340 ft.
(1,000 ft. x .34) less than actual altitude. Thus, if the airplane
lands at an airport with a field elevation of 134 ft., the altimeter
will indicate 206 ft. below sea level (134 ft. airport elevation - 340
ft. altimeter setting error).

question: Under which condition will pressure altitude be equal to true altitude?

answers.A: When indicated altitude is equal to the pressure altitude.
answers.B: When standard atmospheric conditions exist.
answers.C: When the atmospheric pressure is 29.92" Hg.

explanations.A:
because nonstandard temperatures will
make indicated altitude deviate from true altitude.
explanations.B:
Pressure altitude will equal true altitude

when standard atmospheric conditions exist at the current
altitude, ie, 29.92" Hg and 15°C at sea level.
explanations.C:
because, to get true altitude from an
altimeter, both temperature and pressure must be standard.

question: Under what condition is pressure altitude and density altitude the same value?

answers.A: At standard temperature.
answers.B: When indicated, and pressure altitudes are the same value on the altimeter.
answers.C: When the altimeter setting is 29.92" Hg.

explanations.A:
Density altitude, by definition, is pressure
altitude adjusted for nonstandard temperature. Accordingly,
pressure altitude will equal density altitude at standard
temperature.
explanations.B:
because neither indicated nor pressure
altitude is adjusted for nonstandard temperature.
explanations.C:
because pressure altitude has not been
adjusted for nonstandard temperature.

question: Under what condition will true altitude be lower than indicated altitude with an altimeter setting of 29.92" Hg?

answers.A: When density altitude is higher than indicated altitude.
answers.B: In colder than standard air temperature.
answers.C: In warmer than standard air temperature.

explanations.A:
because, assuming an altimeter setting of
29.92, if density altitude is higher than indicated altitude, the air is
thinner and thus warmer. When you are in warmer-than-standard
air, the true altitude is above indicated altitude.
explanations.B:
When temperature lowers en route, you
are lower than your altimeter indicates. Similarly, when you are in

colder-than-standard air temperatures, true altitude is lower than
pressure altitude.
explanations.C:
because, when you are in

warmer-than-standard air, the true altitude is above pressure
altitude.

question: When an altimeter is changed from 30.11" Hg to 29.96" Hg, in which direction will the indicated altitude change and by what value?

answers.B: Altimeter will indicate 150 feet higher.
answers.C: Altimeter will indicate 15 feet lower.
answers.A: Altimeter will indicate 150 feet lower.

explanations.A:
Altimeter settings vary approximately 1"
Hg for each 1,000 ft. of altitude. When the altimeter setting is
changed from 30.11 to 29.96, it is lower by .15" Hg. Thus, the
altimeter will indicate 150 ft. lower (1,000 ft. x .15). Remember
that the indicated altitude and altimeter setting vary directly; i.e.,
when the altimeter setting is adjusted up, indicated altitude
increases and vice versa.
explanations.B:
because, when the altimeter setting is
lowered, indicated altitude decreases, not increases.
explanations.C:
because .15" Hg is equal to 150 ft., not
15 ft.

question: Which condition would cause the altimeter to indicate a lower altitude than actually flown (true altitude)?

answers.A: Air temperature warmer than standard.
answers.B: Atmospheric pressure lower than standard.
answers.C: Air temperature lower than standard.

explanations.A:
When temperatures are warmer than
standard, the pressure levels are raised. That is, the altimeter will
indicate an altitude lower than that at which the aircraft is actually
flying.
explanations.B:
because using the correct altimeter
setting adjusts for nonstandard pressure.
explanations.C:
because in colder-than-standard air,

pressure levels drop. Thus, the altimeter reads higher, not lower,
than true altitude.

question: Which practical test should be made on the electric gyro instruments prior to starting an engine?

answers.A: Check that the attitude of the miniature aircraft is wings level before turning on electrical power.
answers.B: Check that the electrical connections are secure on the back of the instruments.
answers.C: Turn on the electrical power and listen for any unusual or irregular mechanical noise.

explanations.A:
because, due to the construction of the
turn coordinator, the miniature aircraft will be wings level before
turning on the electrical power. Thus, this indication would not be
explanations.B:
because pilots should not be handling or
touching electrical connections behind the instrument panel.
explanations.C:
Electric gyro instruments can be checked
for irregular noises by listening to them after the battery is turned
on but before the engine is started. You should notice any
bearing clatters, clicks, or other unusual noises. Additionally, you
can look at the instruments to see if they are in their expected

Positions. There are additional tests to pursue after the engine is
started.

question: One characteristic that a properly functioning gyro depends upon for operation is the

answers.A: ability to resist precession 90° to any applied force.
answers.B: deflecting force developed from the angular velocity of the spinning wheel.
answers.C: resistance to deflection of the spinning wheel or disc.

explanations.A:
because precession is the name for the
reaction to deflection. The gyro uses precession, not resists it.
explanations.B:
because the deflective force is applied to,
not developed by, the gyro.
explanations.C:
Newton's second law of motion states that
the deflection of a moving body is proportional to the deflective
force applied and is inversely proportional to its weight and
speed. For a gyro, the resistance to deflection is proportional to
the defiective force. This property is used by the attitude indicator.

question: What pre-takeoff check should be made of a vacuum-driven heading indicator in preparation for an IFR flight?

answers.A: After 5 minutes, check that the heading indicator card aligns itself with the magnetic heading of the aircraft.
answers.B: Determine that the heading indicator does not precess more than 2° in 5 minutes of ground operation.
answers.C: After 5 minutes, set the indicator to the magnetic heading of the aircraft and check for proper alignment after taxi turns.

explanations.A:
because non-slaved heading indicators
must be manually set to the correct magnetic heading.
explanations.B:
because a precession error of no more
than 3° in 15 min., not 2° in 5 min., is acceptable for normal
operations.
explanations.C:
Vacuum-driven gyros take several minutes
to get up to speed. After about 5 min., set the heading indicator
to the correct magnetic heading. After taxiing to the runup area,

verify that the heading indicator still indicates the correct
magnetic heading.

question: Clockwise Slave and Free Counterclockwise Adjustment Gyro Pushbutton Adjustment 51. (Refer to figure 143.) The heading on a remote indicating compass is 120 | and the magnetic compass indicates 110 | . What action is required to correctly align the heading indicator with the magnetic compass?

answers.A: Select the free gyro mode and depress the clockwise heading drive button.
answers.B: Select the free gyro mode and depress the counter-clockwise heading drive button.
answers.C: Select the slaved gyro mode and depress the clockwise heading drive button.

explanations.A:
Some remote indicating compasses (RIC)
have a separate slaving control and compensator unit with a
deviation meter. The instrument shows any difference between
the displayed heading and the magnetic heading. It also provides
the controls shown in Fig. 143 to correct any errors. To correct
from 120° indicated on the RIC to the magnetic heading of 110°,
select the free gyro mode and depress the clockwise heading
drive button until 110° heading on RIC is indicated and the
deviation meter is centered.
explanations.B:
because using the counter-clockwise
drive button would increase the indicated headings, e.g., from
120° to 130° indicated.
explanations.C:
because the RIC must be in the free gyro
mode to use the heading drive button.

question: Clockwise Slave and Free Counterclockwise Adjustment Gyro Pushbutton Adjustment 52. (Refer to figure 143.) When the system is in the free gyro mode, depressing the clockwise manual heading drive button will rotate the remote indicating compass card to the

answers.A: right to eliminate right compass card error.
answers.B: left to eliminate left compass card error.
answers.C: right to eliminate left compass card error.

explanations.A:
because you adjust to the right for left, not
right, error.
explanations.B:
because the clockwise manual heading
drive button rotates the compass card to the right, not left.
explanations.C:
A left compass card error means that the
card has rotated too far to the left; i-e., it reads too higha
heading. The clockwise adjustment rotates the indicating
compass card to the right to eliminate left compass card error.
For example, this would change a 120° heading to 110°.

question: Clockwise Slave and Free Counterclockwise Adjustment Gyro Pushbutton Adjustment 53. (Refer to figure 143.) The heading on a remote indicating compass is 5° to the left of that desired. What action is required to move the desired heading under the heading reference?

answers.A: Select the free gyro mode and depress the counter-clockwise heading drive button.
answers.B: Select the slaved gyro mode and depress the clockwise heading drive button.
answers.C: Select the free gyro mode and depress the clockwise heading drive button.

explanations.A:
If the heading on the compass is left of that
desired, the compass has rotated too far to the right, whichis a
right compass error. Thus, the slaving control must be placed in
the free mode, and the counterclockwise drive button must be
depressed.
explanations.B:
because the RIC must be in the free gyro
mode to use the heading drive button and the counterclockwise
heading drive button should be depressed.
explanations.C:
because the clockwise heading drive
button would correct a left, not a right, card error.

question: What pre-takeoff check should be made of the attitude indicator in preparation for an IFR flight?

answers.A: The miniature airplane should erect and become stable within 5 minutes.
answers.B: The horizon bar does not vibrate during warmup.
answers.C: The horizon bar should erect and become stable within 5 minutes.

explanations.A:
because the miniature airplane can be
adjusted manually but otherwise remains stationary. It is the
horizon bar that moves within the instrument face.
explanations.B:
because the horizon bar usually vibrates
during warm-up as the gyro gets up to speed.
explanations.C:
The pretakeoff check for attitude indicators
is that, within the 5-min. warm-up, the horizon bar should erect to
the horizontal position and remain at the correct position. It
should remain stable during straight taxiing and taxi turns.

question: Which condition during taxi is an indication that an attitude indicator is unreliable?

answers.A: The horizon bar vibrates during warmup.
answers.B: The horizon bar does not align itself with the miniature airplane after warmup.
answers.C: The horizon bar tilts more than 5° while making taxi turns.

explanations.A:
because the horizon bar will vibrate as
the gyros get up to speed during warm-up.
explanations.B:
because the horizon bar aligns itself with
the center of the dial, indicating level flight. Then the miniature
airplane must be adjusted to align with the horizon bar from the
pilot's perspective.
explanations.C:
The horizon bar in an attitude indicator
should not tilt more than 5° during a taxi turn. If it does, itis
unreliable and should not be used for IFR flight.

question: During coordinated turns, which force moves the pendulous vanes of a vacuum-driven attitude indicator resulting in precession of the gyro toward the inside of the turn?

answers.A: Centrifugal.
answers.B: Acceleration.
answers.C: Deceleration.

explanations.A:
The attitude indicator normally erects itself

by discharging air equally through four exhaust ports, each of
which is partially covered by a pendulous vane. During

coordinated (and skidding) turns, centrifugal force moves the
vanes from their vertical position, precessing the gyro toward the
inside of the turn.
explanations.B:
because acceleration is a force that
induces climb/descent errors in the attitude indicator.
explanations.C:
because deceleration is a force that
induces climb/descent errors in the attitude indicator.

question: Ifa 180° steep turn is made to the right and the aircraft is rolled out to ‘straight-and-level flight by visual references, the attitude indicator

answers.A: show a slight skid and climb to the right.
answers.B: may show a slight climb and turn.
answers.C: should immediately show straight-and-level flight.

explanations.A:
because evidence of a skid error cannot
be read from the attitude indicator, and the turn error would be to
the left, not to the right.
explanations.B:
In 180° coordinated steep turns, when the
airplane is rolled out to straight-and-level flight, the attitude
indicator will indicate a turn to the opposite direction along with a
slight climb.
explanations.C:
because, when the airplane is rolled out
of a coordinated 180° steep turn to straight-and-level flight, the

attitude indicator will indicate a turn to the opposite direction with

question: During normal coordinated turns, what error due to precession should you observe when rolling out to straight-and-level flight from a 180° steep turn to the right?

answers.A: The miniature aircraft would show a slight turn indication to the left.
answers.B: The miniature aircraft would show a slight descent and wings-level attitude.
answers.C: A straight-and-level coordinated flight indication.

explanations.A:
In 180° coordinated steep turns, when the
airplane is rolled out to straight-and-level flight, the attitude
indicator will indicate a turn to the opposite direction along with a
slight climb. Thus, the indicated turn would be to the left if the
steep turn were made to the right.
explanations.B: because it will indicate a slight climb, not
explanations.C:
because the attitude indicator will show a

slight climb to the left, not straight-and-level flight, and it does not
indicate coordinated flight.

question: During normal operation of a vacuum-driven attitude indicator, what attitude indication should you see when rolling out from a 180° skidding turn to straight-and-level coordinated flight?

answers.A: Anose-high indication relative to level flight.
answers.B: The miniature aircraft shows a turn in the direction opposite the skid.
answers.C: A straight-and-level coordinated flight indication.

explanations.A:
because a nose-high indication will result
only when the aircraft is rolling out of a coordinated turn.
explanations.B:
Similarly to coordinated turns, the attitude
indicator will show a bank in the opposite direction when the
aircraft is rolled out of a skidding turn. However, there will be no
nose-up indication.
explanations.C:
because the attitude indicator will show a
slight turn in the opposite direction, not straight-and-level flight,
and it does not indicate coordinated flight.

question: Errors in both pitch and bank indication on an attitude indicator are usually at a maximum as the aircraft rolls out of a

answers.B: 360° turn.
answers.C: 180° turn.

explanations.A:
because pitch and bank errors are usually
the greatest after 180°, not 270°, of turn.
explanations.B:
because pitch and bank errors are usually
the greatest after 180°, not 360°, of turn.
explanations.C:
Errors for both pitch and bank indication
on an attitude indicator are greatest when rolling out of a 180°
turn. This precession error, normally between 3° and 5°, is
self-correcting by the part of the heading indicator called the
erecting mechanism.

question: When an aircraft is decelerated, some attitude indicators will precess and incorrectly indicate a

answers.B: climb.
answers.C: descent.
answers.A: left turn.

explanations.A:
because acceleration and deceleration
result in erroneous pitch readings, not turning errors.
explanations.B:
because acceleration, not deceleration,
may result in precession-related errors indicating a climb.
explanations.C:
Deceleration affects some attitude
indicators through precession to incorrectly indicate a descent.

question: When an aircraft is accelerated, some attitude indicators will precess and incorrectly indicate a

answers.A: climb.
answers.B: descent.
answers.C: right turn.

explanations.A:
Acceleration affects some attitude
indicators through precession to incorrectly indicate a climb.
explanations.B:
because deceleration, not acceleration,
may result in precession-related errors indicating a descent.
explanations.C:
because acceleration and deceleration
result in erroneous pitch readings, not turning errors.

question: Prior to starting an engine, you should check the turn-and-slip indicator to determine if the

answers.A: ball will move freely from one end of the tube to the other when the aircraft is rocked.
answers.B: needle is approximately centered and the tube is full of fluid.
answers.C: needle indication properly corresponds to the angle of the wings or rotors with the horizon.

explanations.A:
because rocking the aircraft is not
necessary. Freedom of movement of the ball is checked during
taxi.
explanations.B:
Prior to starting an engine, you should
determine that the needle of the turn-and-slip indicator is
approximately centered and that the tube is full of fluid with the
ball also approximately centered if the airplane is ona level
surface.
explanations.C:
because the needle corresponds to rate
and direction of turn, not wing or rotor angle.

question: What indications should you observe on the turn-and-slip indicator during taxi?

answers.A: The ball moves freely opposite the turn, and the needle deflects in the direction of the turn.
answers.B: The ball deflects opposite the turn, but the needle remains centered.
answers.C: The needle deflects in the direction of the turn, but the ball remains centered.

explanations.A:
During taxi, the turn-and-slip indicator ball
should move freely opposite the direction of any turn since
centrifugal force forces the ball to the outside. Also, the rate of
turn indicator should indicate a turn in the proper direction.
explanations.B:
because the needle deflects in the
direction of the turn.
explanations.C:
because the ball will deflect opposite to
the direction of the turn.

question: What indications are displayed by the miniature aircraft of a turn coordinator?

answers.A: Indirect indication of bank angle and pitch attitude.
answers.B: Direct indication of bank angle and pitch attitude.
answers.C: Rate of roll and rate of turn.

explanations.A:
because the turn coordinator has no
felationship to pitch attitude.
explanations.B:
because the turn coordinator only

indirectly indicates bank angle and has no relationship to pitch
attitude.
explanations.C:
The turn coordinator indicates rate of roll
and rate of turn. When the bank is constant, the rate of turnis

indicated. When the bank is changing, the rate of roll is also
indicated.

question: What does the miniature aircraft of the turn coordinator directly display?

answers.B: Angle of bank.
answers.C: Angle of bank and rate of turn.
answers.A: Rate of roll and rate of turn.

explanations.A:
The turn coordinator indicates rate of roll
and rate of turn. When the bank is constant, the rate of turn is
indicated. When the bank is changing, the rate of roll is also
indicated.
explanations.B:
because the angle of bank is not directly
indicated by the turn coordinator.
explanations.C:
because the angle of bank is not directly
indicated by the turn coordinator.

question: What indication is presented by the miniature aircraft of the turn coordinator?

answers.A: Direct indication of the bank attitude and the quality of the turn.
answers.B: Indirect indication of the bank attitude.
answers.C: Quality of the turn.

explanations.A:
because the turn coordinator does NOT
provide a direct indication of bank.
explanations.B:
The miniature aircraft of the turn
coordinator indicates the rate of roll when bank is changing.
When the rotation around the longitudinal axis is zero, the
instrument indicates the rate of turn. Thus, it provides only an
indirect indication of the angle of bank.
explanations.C:
because the ball in the turn coordinator,

not the miniature aircraft, provides information on the quality of
the turn.

question: The displacement of a turn coordinator during a coordinated turn will

answers.A: indicate the angle of bank.
answers.B: increase as angle of bank increases.
answers.C: remain constant for a given bank regardless of airspeed.

explanations.A:
because the angle of bank is only
indirectly indicated.
explanations.B:
The displacement of a turn coordinator

increases as angle of bank (in coordinated flight) increases

because the turn coordinator shows rate of turn, which increases
as angle of bank increases.
explanations.C:
because, when the rate of roll is zero, the
turn coordinator provides information concerning the rate of turn,

which in turn changes as airspeed changes given a constant
bank.

question: What indication should be observed on a turn coordinator during a left turn while taxiing?

answers.B: Both the miniature aircraft and the ball will remain centered.
answers.C: The miniature aircraft will show a turn to the left and the ball moves to the right.
answers.A: The miniature aircraft will show a turn to the left and the ball remains centered.

explanations.A:
because the ball moves to the outside of
the turn due to centrifugal force.
explanations.B:
because the miniature aircraft reacts to

yaw and shows a tum to the left, and the ball reacts to centrifugal
force by moving right.
explanations.C:
On a taxiing turn to the left, the turn
coordinator shows a turn to the left, and the ball moves to the
right. The centrifugal force of the turn, which is not offset by bank
when taxiing, forces the ball opposite to the turn.
